lesson.summary: How to say "I am", "you are", "she is" and so on with być (to be), and when to use the little words ja, ty, on, ona.
body: {{Być}} means "to be", and it changes its ending for each person: {{jestem}} (I am), {{jesteś}} (you are), {{jest}} (he, she or it is), {{jesteśmy}} (we are), {{jesteście}} (you all are), {{są}} (they are). Because the ending already tells you who is meant, Polish usually drops the pronoun: {{Jestem w domu.}} is "I'm at home". Saying {{Ja jestem w domu.}} is not wrong, but it sounds like you are stressing "I".

So keep the pronoun only for contrast or emphasis: {{Ja jestem w domu, a ty?}} ("I'm at home, and you?"). The pronouns are {{ja}} (I), {{ty}} (you, one person), {{on}} (he), {{ona}} (she), {{ono}} (it), {{my}} (we), {{wy}} (you, more than one), and two words for "they": {{oni}} and {{one}}.
more: {{Oni}} is "they" for any group with at least one man in it ({{rodzice}}, {{brat i siostra}}). {{One}} is for groups with no men: women only, children, animals or things ({{mama i babcia}}, {{klucze}}).
Polish has no word for the "it" in "it's cold": just say {{Jest zimno.}} The same goes for {{Jest późno.}} ("It's late").
To introduce people or things, use {{to jest}} ("this is") for one and {{to są}} ("these are") for more: {{To jest moja mama.}}, {{To są moi rodzice.}} The word {{to}} here never changes.

With her parents and other older people you may use the polite {{pan}} (sir) and {{pani}} (madam) instead of {{ty}}. They take the "he/she" form of the verb: {{Pani jest bardzo miła.}} ("You are very kind").

When "to be" is followed by a noun on its own, as in "I am a teacher", Polish puts that noun in a different case (the instrumental), which comes later. Until then, stick to {{być}} with places ({{w domu}}), describing words ({{zmęczony}}) and {{to jest}}.

lesson.summary: Every Polish noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, and you can usually tell which from its last letter.
body: Gender matters because the little words around a noun change to match it: "my" is {{mój}}, {{moja}} or {{moje}}, "this" is {{ten}}, {{ta}} or {{to}}, and describing words end in -y/-i, -a or -e. Luckily the ending of the noun (in its dictionary form) usually tells you the gender. A consonant at the end means masculine: {{dom}}, {{stół}}, {{chleb}}. An -a means feminine: {{kawa}}, {{kuchnia}}, {{mama}}. An -o, -e, -ę or -um means neuter: {{piwo}}, {{mieszkanie}}, {{imię}}, {{muzeum}}.

There are a few exceptions worth learning now. Words for men are masculine even when they end in -a: {{mężczyzna}} (man), {{tata}} (dad), and men's names like {{Kuba}}. And some feminine nouns end in a consonant, for example {{noc}} (night), {{rzecz}} (thing), {{wieś}} (village), {{mysz}} (mouse) and {{kość}} (bone).

table.caption: Ending, gender, and the words that match
head: Ending
Gender
"my"
"this"

more: "Your" (to one person) works the same way as "my": {{twój}}, {{twoja}}, {{twoje}}.

Describing words follow the same three-way pattern: {{dobry chleb}}, {{dobra kawa}}, {{dobre piwo}}. Some masculine forms end in -i instead of -y, such as {{wysoki}} (tall), but the feminine is still -a ({{wysoka}}) and the neuter -e ({{wysokie}}).

Nouns ending in -ość are feminine: {{miłość}} (love), {{radość}} (joy). The one everyday exception is {{gość}} (guest), which is masculine. A few nouns that end in -i are feminine too, the most useful being {{pani}}.
Don't mix up {{to}} meaning "this" with a neuter noun ({{to piwo}}) and {{to jest}} meaning "this is". In {{To jest moja mama.}} the {{to}} never changes, whatever the gender.
If you meet a noun ending in a soft consonant (like -ć, -ść, -ń or -ś) and are not sure, check the dictionary: some are masculine ({{dzień}}, {{gość}}) and some feminine ({{kość}}, {{wieś}}).
A few words break the -um rule: {{album}} is masculine (mój album).

lesson.summary: Most Polish verbs follow one of three patterns in the present tense; learn the "I" and "you" forms and the rest falls into place.
body: A Polish verb changes its ending to show who is doing something, so the pronoun is usually dropped: {{mam}} is "I have", {{masz}} is "you have". Most verbs belong to one of three groups. Group one has "I" in -am and "you" in -asz: {{mam, masz}}, {{czytam, czytasz}}, {{znam, znasz}}. Group two has -ę and -esz: {{piszę, piszesz}}, {{piję, pijesz}}, {{idę, idziesz}}. Group three has -ę and -isz or -ysz: {{mówię, mówisz}}, {{robię, robisz}}, {{słyszę, słyszysz}}.

The "he/she" form is the "you" form without the final -sz: {{masz}} → {{ma}}, {{piszesz}} → {{pisze}}, {{mówisz}} → {{mówi}}. "We" adds -my and "you all" adds -cie to that: {{mamy, macie}}, {{piszemy, piszecie}}, {{mówimy, mówicie}}. "They" ends in -ą (or -ają in group one): {{mają}}, {{piszą}}, {{mówią}}.
more: You can't always tell the group from the infinitive, so learn each new verb with its "I" and "you" forms. Many verbs in -ować change -owa- to -uj-: -uję, -ujesz: {{pracować}} → {{pracuję, pracujesz}}, {{gotować}} → {{gotuję}}, {{kupować}} → {{kupuję}}.

In group two the stem sometimes changes between "I" and "you": {{idę, idziesz}} (go on foot), {{jadę, jedziesz}} (go by vehicle), {{biorę, bierzesz}} (take). The "they" form goes back to the "I" stem: {{idą}}, {{jadą}}, {{biorą}}.

A few very common verbs have -em, -esz: {{rozumiem, rozumiesz}} (understand), and they work like group one ({{rozumiemy, rozumiecie}}, but "they" is {{rozumieją}}). {{Jeść}} (eat) and {{wiedzieć}} (know a fact) are irregular: {{jem, jesz, je}} and {{wiem, wiesz, wie}}.
Polish has one present tense for both "I drink" and "I'm drinking": {{Piję kawę.}} covers both.

topics.title: Accusative after mam, lubię, chcę, widzę

lesson.summary: After verbs like mam, lubię, chcę and widzę, the thing you have, like, want or see changes its ending (the accusative case).
body: In {{Lubię kawę}} ("I like coffee"), {{kawa}} has become {{kawę}}. That is the accusative: the form of a noun when it is the direct object of a verb such as {{mam}} (I have), {{lubię}} (I like), {{chcę}} (I want), {{widzę}} (I see), {{kocham}} (I love), {{jem}} (I eat) or {{piję}} (I drink).

The good news: only two groups change. Feminine nouns in -a swap it for -ę ({{woda}} → {{wodę}}). Masculine nouns for people and animals add -a ({{brat}} → {{brata}}, {{kot}} → {{kota}}). Masculine things and all neuter nouns stay exactly as they are ({{Mam dom}}, {{Lubię piwo}}).

head: Kind of noun
Dictionary form
Accusative

more: Some masculine words lose an e when they add an ending: {{pies}} → {{psa}}, {{dziadek}} → {{dziadka}}, {{wujek}} → {{wujka}}. You just learn these as you meet them.
Men's words that end in -a behave like feminine nouns here: {{tata}} → {{tatę}}. Feminine nouns that do not end in -a usually stay the same: {{Masz sól?}}
Animals count as "alive" even on your plate: {{Jem kurczaka}} (I'm eating chicken).

With {{chcę}} and with food and drink, Polish often uses a different form meaning "some": {{Chcesz ciasta?}} (Do you want some cake?). Both {{Chcesz ciasto?}} and {{Chcesz ciasta?}} are fine; the next topic explains that -a/-y form.

lesson.summary: When you put nie in front of a verb like mam, lubię or widzę, the object switches to the genitive case, and nie ma means "there isn't".
body: To make a sentence negative, put {{nie}} before the verb: {{Mam czas}} → {{Nie mam czasu}}. Notice that the object changed too. After a negated verb, the thing you don't have, like or see goes into the genitive: feminine -a becomes -y or -i ({{kawa}} → {{kawy}}), neuter -o or -e becomes -a ({{mleko}} → {{mleka}}), and masculine nouns add -a or -u ({{brat}} → {{brata}}, {{czas}} → {{czasu}}).
{{Nie ma}} on its own means "there isn't" or "isn't here", and it takes the genitive as well: {{Nie ma chleba}} (There's no bread), {{Nie ma taty}} (Dad isn't here).
more: Masculine -a or -u? Masculine people and animals always take -a ({{brata}}, {{psa}}, {{kota}}). Men's words ending in -a, like {{tata}}, take -y instead, like feminine nouns ({{taty}}). For things there is no reliable rule: {{chleba}}, {{sera}}, {{klucza}} but {{czasu}}, {{soku}}, {{telefonu}}, {{samochodu}}. Learn each one with its genitive.
Feminine nouns take -i instead of -y after k, g and soft sounds: {{babcia}} → {{babci}}, {{łazienka}} → {{łazienki}}, {{sól}} → {{soli}}.
For masculine people and animals the genitive looks the same as the accusative, so {{Widzę brata}} and {{Nie widzę brata}} use the same word.
Only the direct object switches. Verbs that use another case keep it when negated, and {{nie jestem}} works differently; that comes later.

lesson.summary: Adjectives change their ending to match the gender of the noun they describe: -y/-i, -a or -e.
body: Polish adjectives match their noun. With a masculine noun they end in -y ({{dobry dom}}), with a feminine noun in -a ({{dobra kawa}}), and with a neuter noun in -e ({{dobre piwo}}). This works whether the adjective comes before the noun or after {{jest}}: {{Zupa jest pyszna}}.
The same goes for you. A man says {{Jestem zmęczony}} (I'm tired) and a woman says {{Jestem zmęczona}}. So when you ask her, it's {{Jesteś zmęczona?}}, and she'll answer with the feminine form too.
more: After k and g the masculine ending is -i and the neuter ending is -ie: {{drogi}}, {{drogie}}; {{wysoki}}, {{wysokie}}. A few adjectives are soft and keep an i in every form: {{tani}}, {{tania}}, {{tanie}} (cheap).
Agreement follows the real gender of the word, not just its look: {{tata}} ends in -a but is a man, so {{Tata jest zmęczony}}.
In the plural, -e is used for everything except groups including men: {{Okna są duże}}, but {{Rodzice są zmęczeni}}. Masculine plurals for people change in other ways too; that comes later.

lesson.summary: How to ask yes/no questions and questions with what, who, where, when, how, why and how much.
body: Yes/no questions are easy in Polish: take an ordinary sentence and either raise your voice at the end ({{Masz czas?}}) or put {{czy}} in front ({{Czy masz czas?}}). There is no "do" and no swapping of words: the statement stays exactly as it is.

For other questions, put the question word first and keep the rest in normal order: {{Gdzie mieszkasz?}} (Where do you live?), {{Co robisz?}} (What are you doing?). Polish has three words for "where": {{gdzie}} (at which place), {{skąd}} (from where) and {{dokąd}} (where to).
more: In everyday speech {{czy}} is often left out and the rising voice does the work. It is more common in careful or polite speech, and with older relatives: {{Czy mogę pomóc?}}
Kto and co change form like nouns: {{z kim}} (with whom), {{kogo}} (whom), {{czego}} (of what). For now just learn {{Z kim?}} as a phrase.

For clock times use {{O której?}} (at what time?) rather than kiedy. {{Jaki}} (what kind of) and {{który}} (which) agree with the noun like adjectives: {{Która godzina?}}, {{Jaki to film?}} {{Czyj}} (whose) agrees in the same way: {{czyj}} with a masculine noun, {{czyja}} with a feminine one.
You can also tag {{prawda?}} or {{tak?}} onto a statement to check something: {{Jesteś w domu, prawda?}}

lesson.summary: How to say what you did as a man (-łem) and ask her what she did (-łaś).
body: To make the past tense, take the infinitive, drop the -ć and add ł plus an ending: {{robić}} → {{robił}}-. The ending shows both the person and the gender. As a man you say {{byłem}}, {{robiłem}} (I was, I did). When you ask her, it is {{byłaś}}, {{robiłaś}} (you were, you did). She says {{byłam}} about herself and asks you {{byłeś}}?
Questions need no extra word like English "did": {{Spałaś dobrze?}} is literally "you slept well?" said with a rising voice. For he, she and it there is no person ending: {{był}}, {{była}}, {{było}}.

table.caption: Past tense of być and robić
head: man
woman

more: For "it" (neuter nouns like {{wino}}) the ending is -ło: {{Wino było dobre.}}
In the singular, verbs ending in -eć usually change e to a before the ł: {{myśleć}} → {{myślałem}}, {{widzieć}} → {{widziałem}}, {{chcieć}} → {{chciałem}}, {{mieć}} → {{miałem}}.
A few common verbs are irregular. {{iść}} (go on foot): {{szedłem}}, {{szłam}}, {{szedłeś}}, {{szłaś}}. {{jeść}} (eat): {{jadłem}}, {{jadłam}}. {{móc}} (can): {{mogłem}}, {{mogłam}}, but he {{mógł}}.

Most verbs come in pairs. The imperfective ({{robiłem}}, {{dzwoniłem}}) describes an activity or something ongoing or repeated: "I was doing, I used to call". The perfective ({{zrobiłem}}, {{zadzwoniłem}}, {{kupiłem}}) describes one finished action: "I did it, I called, I bought". Either is a real past tense; you will pick up the pairs over time.
